description: We are Totally Spies, a team of four girls who love uncovering hidden stories. For this mission, we went undercover in NASA’s archives to find the machines humanity left behind on the Moon and Mars. We combine storytelling, design, code and sound to turn space data into adventures young explorers will remember.
summary: With Abandoned, Not Forgotten, we wanted the machines left on the Moon and Mars to tell their own stories, to kids aged 10 to 16 and to anyone curious about space exploration and its history. Our project addresses the “Abandon Not Forgotten” challenge by combining NASA mission data with interactive 3D globes, first-person storytelling, narration and simple language for young learners. Each rover, lander and helicopter shares what it did and why it was left behind, which makes space history personal and memorable. It’s a field trip to other worlds, designed for classrooms, libraries and curious minds at home.
details:
Details

Abandoned, Not Forgotten is an interactive 3D website that takes kids aged 10 to 16 on a field trip to the machines humanity left behind on the Moon and Mars. Explorers choose a world, ride through a launch countdown, and land on a 3D globe they can spin and zoom. Glowing markers sit at each machine’s real landing coordinates, and a little astronaut walks over to whichever one you pick.

Each machine opens a story card with a spinning 3D model and six short tabs: About, Function, Launch, Mission, Abandoned and Why? With sound on, a narrator reads each tab while the text types out like a radio transmission. A “Next stop” button guides explorers through the machines in the order they arrived, a “Machines found” counter turns each visited marker green, and soft space sounds set the mood.

Benefits and intended impact

Space history usually comes as dates and numbers. We turn it into stories: why Surveyor 3 bounced twice, how Spirit kept exploring on a broken wheel, why the Moon Buggies are still parked up there. Kids learn real science and history while having fun, and we hope they leave curious about what we’ll explore, and leave behind.

Tools we used

  • Figma Make to prototype the design
  • React, TypeScript and Vite for the website, written in VS Code
  • Three.js (with React Three Fiber) for the 3D globes and markers
  • Google’s model-viewer for the rotating 3D equipment models
  • Narakeet to create the voice narration for each story section
  • NASA 3D Resources models and NASA mission archives for our facts and coordinates
  • GitHub to work together as a team
  • Claude for coding, debugging, and troubleshooting
  • Vercel to host and deploy the website

What makes it creative

Instead of a museum label, each machine tells its own story in its own voice. The site feels like a mission: a helmet-visor display, a countdown, radio beeps, and text that arrives like a live transmission.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: facts come from NASA sources, and we mark approximate locations as approximate.
  • Age-appropriate: short, simple sentences with fun details for 10 to 16 year olds.
  • Accessibility: the text appears alongside the audio, sound is off until you turn it on, the site respects reduced-motion settings, and it works on phones.
  • Teamwork: we split the work across story, code and audio, and shared it through GitHub.
